sentences.text: You studied for hours, you read every page, and a week later, almost none of it is still in your head.
This is not because you are lazy, and it is not because your memory is broken.
It is because most of us study in the exact way that brains forget fastest.
Meet Sam.
Sam reads a chapter three times, highlights half of it, and feels great about it.
Two weeks later, Sam stares at an exam question and thinks, I have never seen this before.
In the next eight minutes, I will show you why that happens and six fixes that actually work.
One of them feels almost unfair because it works so well, I will save it for number two.
In 1885, a German psychologist named Herman Ebbinghaus decided to test his own memory.
He memorized lists of meaningless syllables, then checked how many he could still recall later.
He repeated this again and again for years with nobody to help him.
What he found became famous, we call it the forgetting curve.
Right after learning, you remember a lot, then memory drops quickly and later the loss slows down.
Most of the loss happens early in the first hours and days.
So if you never go back to what you learned, the curve simply takes it.
Notice what this means.
Forgetting is not a bug.
Your brain forgets on purpose because it cannot keep everything.
It keeps what you use and let's go of what you do not.
So the real question is how to prove to your brain that something is worth keeping.
Here is the good news.
Every time you bring a memory back, the curve gets flatter.
Think of a path in a forest.
Walk it once and the grass grows back.
Walk it every week and it becomes a road.
That is the secret behind everything that follows.
Let's start with the biggest trap of all.
Fix number one.
Stop rereading your notes.
Rereading feels productive.
The words look familiar and familiar feels like knowing.
Psychologists call this the illusion of knowing.
You recognize the page, but you could not produce the answer.
Highlighting has the same problem.
A large review of study techniques rated both of them as low and usefulness.
That does not mean they are useless.
It means they are a weak use of your time.
A better question to ask yourself is not, do I recognize this?
It is, can I produce this?
Here is something strange you will notice as we go.
The methods that work feel harder and the methods that fail feel easier.
Sam's problem was never effort.
Sam worked hard, but on the wrong kind of work.
Imagine reading a recipe 10 times.
You still could not cook the dish without looking.
Cooking it once from memory teaches you more.
Fix number two.
Test yourself before you feel ready.
Close the book.
Take a blank page.
Write down everything you can remember.
Studying biology instead of rereading the chapter on the heart, cover it up, draw the heart from memory and label every part you can.
Then open the book and check what you missed.
This is called retrieval practice, and it is one of the best studied effects in learning research.
In classic experiments, students who practiced recalling material often remembered more a week later than students who simply reread it.
Even a wrong guess helps because the right answer sticks better afterwards.
Flashcards work for exactly this reason, but only if you answer before you flip the card.
If it feels a little hard good, that feeling is the learning.
Researchers have a name for this.
They call it a desirable difficulty.
The effort you feel is not a warning sign.
It is the signal that learning is happening.
Sam tries it.
On the first attempt, Sam remembers four things out of 20.
That feels terrible, but now Sam knows exactly what to study.
Fix number three.
Spread it out.
Studying the same topic for five hours in one night feels intense, but it mostly builds short term memory.
Cramming can get you through tomorrow's test.
It rarely survives until next month.
Spaced repetition means you review something just as you are about to forget it.
For example, review it the next day, then three days later, then a week later, then a month later.
Each review is a retrieval, so each one flattens the forgetting curve a little more.
Several short sessions usually beat one long session, even when the total time is the same.
The sweet spot is to review when remembering feels slightly hard, but not impossible.
Here is a rule of thumb.
The longer you want to remember something, the longer the gaps between reviews can be.
And they fit into a busy week much more easily than one giant night.
Apps like Anki can schedule the reviews for you, but a simple calendar works too.
Quick pause.
So far, stop rereading, test yourself and spread it out.
Three more to go and the next one feels backwards.
Fix number four, mix it up.
Most people practice one type of problem until it feels easy and then move on.
That is called blocked practice.
Interleaving means mixing different types of problems in the same session.
It feels worse.
You make more mistakes while you practice.
But later on a real test, mixed practice usually wins because you learn to choose the right method, not just repeat one.
In one well -known study, people learn to recognize painting styles better when the artists were mixed together.
Doing math makes different problem types, learning a language, mixed vocabulary, listening and speaking.
Preparing for a physics exam shuffled the problems from every chapter together instead of finishing one chapter at a time.
Research on motor skills points the same way from basketball drills to piano scales.
Fix number five, sleep is part of studying.
While you sleep, your brain replays and stabilizes what you learned during the day.
People who sleep after learning usually remember more than people who stay awake for the same stretch of time.
So the all -nighter is a trap.
You give up the very thing that locks memories in for a few extra hours.
A better plan is to study in the evening, review briefly in the morning, and protect your sleep.
A short nap after learning can help too, but nothing replaces a full night.
And a tired brain does not just remember less.
It also struggles to take in anything new.
Fix number six, explain it like you are teaching a 10 -year -old.
Pick a concept, explain it out loud in simple words with no note.
The moment you get stuck, you have found a gap in your understanding.
Go back, fill the gap, and try again.
Some people call this the Feynman technique, named after the physicist Richard Feynman.
You can explain to a friend, a pet, or an empty chair.
Teaching is just retrieval with a purpose.
Try it with something you think you already know.
You may be surprised how fast the confident explanation falls apart.
One more tip, connect new facts to things you already know.
Add a picture or a little story.
Connected facts are easier to retrieve because your brain has more paths leading to them.
Now let's test you.
Without scrolling back, name three of the six fixes.
Go ahead, I will wait.
Here they are.
Stop rereading, test yourself, spread it out, mix it up, sleep, and teach it.
Now let's put it into a simple weekly routine.
Study something new on Monday.
On Tuesday, close the book and write down what you remember.
On Thursday, quiz yourself again and mix in older topics.
Next week, explain it out loud and sleep well every night in between.
Sam follows this for a month.
The exam arrives and Sam is calm because every question looks familiar for the right reason.
Your memory is not broken.
It is doing exactly what it was built to do, which is to forget whatever seems unimportant.
Retrieval, spacing, mixing, sleep, and teaching are how you tell your brain.
This one matters.
Do not try all six at once.
Pick one, make it a habit for two weeks and then add the next.
And here is a challenge.
Come back to this video in three days and try to list all six fixes without looking.
That is spaced retrieval in action.
Try just one fix this week and tell me in the comments which one you chose.
Because the person who remembers the most is not the one who studies the longest.
It is the one who tries to remember.
